**Ch 001 Draft**

The paragraph beginning "There was something pathetic in his concentration… When the telephone rang inside and the butler left the porch Daisy seized upon the momentary interruption and leaned towards me" is worth examining. The draft cut the butler's-nose anecdote (authorized digression removal), so Daisy's "leaning toward" Nick has no setup — but the passage that follows describes only light on her face and gives no content of what she said, then transitions smoothly to the butler returning. No genuine confusion results; the reader understands she leaned in during the interruption.

The "fifth guest's shrill metallic urgency" reference — the phone call has been established in the draft, so this reads fine.

"She's going to spend lots of weekends out here this summer" / Nick looking after Jordan — Jordan's golf-cheating subplot is authorized removed, but Jordan herself is present and named in the draft, so this is just a less-detailed version.

**Ch 002 Draft**

"The sister sat down beside me on the couch" / later "the sister leaned close and whispered: 'Neither of them can stand the person they're married to. It's really his wife that's keeping them apart.'"

The second passage is structurally damaged. In the source, Catherine says "Neither of them can stand the person they're married to" — and the referent "them" is clearly Tom and Myrtle. But this statement follows naturally from a long dialogue passage about divorce and marriage. In the draft, however, between Catherine's gossip about Gatsby and this whispered line, there is a jump: "Why did you, Myrtle?" the sister demanded." — This question about why Myrtle married Wilson arrives with no preceding dialogue that prompted it. In the source it arises from a specific exchange: Catherine says "She really ought to get away from him… Tom's the first sweetie she ever had," then Myrtle's declaration about marrying Wilson, then Catherine's "Why did you, Myrtle?" In the draft, the whispered line about "neither of them" is immediately followed by "Daisy was not a Catholic" (which works) and then "Why did you, Myrtle?" with no triggering exchange. That question is a reply whose setup was cut.

"Taking my hat from the chandelier, I followed the photographer out." — In the source, Mr. McKee's departure is described in detail, and Nick follows him. In the draft, "the photographer" has been introduced earlier as "a pale photographer from below" — the reader can connect this. Not a finding.

"'Come to lunch some day,' he suggested as we groaned down in the elevator." — In the draft Mr. McKee (the photographer) was introduced without his name, as "a pale photographer from below." The dialogue attribution "he suggested" has no named antecedent — but the draft reader knows it is the photographer Nick just followed out. Marginal, but the reader can infer.

The real structural damage is the unattributed/broken dialogue:
